usage: The person you love takes 을/를 (object marker), never 에 — 사랑하다 is a transitive verb that acts directly on a person.
The fixed idiom uses the noun 사랑 + 에 빠지다 ('fall into love'); here 사랑 is a noun, so don't conjugate it as a verb.
사랑해 주세요 asks someone to direct their love toward another, e.g. a fan telling an idol 우리 가수 많이 사랑해 주세요.
진심으로 ('from the heart') is the natural adverb that intensifies 사랑하다 without sounding theatrical.
examples: 저는 가족을 사랑해요
I love my family
The neutral polite 해요 form — safe for almost any listener and the default for stating affection plainly.
나는 너를 사랑해
I love you
반말: 너를 ('you') plus bare 사랑해 marks intimacy, used only with a partner or someone very close.
우리 부모님은 서로를 평생 사랑하셨어요
My parents loved each other their whole lives
Honorific 시 (사랑하셨어요) raises the subject (parents), and 서로를 supplies the mutual object.
nuance: 사랑하다 is the weightiest love verb in Korean, covering romantic love, family love, and devotion to a cause; it is far heavier than English 'love you', which English speakers toss off to friends and even food. The honest near-synonyms split by intensity: 좋아하다 means 'like / have a crush on' and is what you confess at the start of a relationship (너 좋아해 = 'I like you'), while 사랑하다 is reserved for committed, serious feeling — saying 사랑해 too early can feel startling. Because it is a 하다 verb, the stem 하 + 여 always contracts to 해, giving 사랑해요 and past 사랑했어요 (never 사랑하요/사랑하았어요); the future and modal forms keep 하 (사랑할 거예요, 사랑해야 해요). The object of love takes 을/를, so the classic pitfall is writing 엄마에게 사랑해요 by copying English 'love TO someone' — Korean loves the person directly: 엄마를 사랑해요. Natural partners include 진심으로 사랑하다, 죽도록 사랑하다, and the noun idiom 사랑에 빠지다.
mistakes: Writing 사랑하요 instead of 사랑해요 — every 하다 verb contracts 하 + 여 to 해, so the polite form must be 사랑해요.
Marking the beloved with 에/에게 (사랑에게) by analogy with English 'love to' — the person you love is a direct object and takes 을/를: 너를 사랑해.
Using 사랑하다 for casual 'I love this food/song' — Koreans say 좋아하다 there; 사랑하다 about objects sounds melodramatic.

usage: The target of hatred takes 을/를; 미워하다 attaches to a person, not an abstract thing.
Negative command 미워하지 마(세요) is how you ask someone to stop resenting you.
서로 ('each other') turns it mutual; common when talking about a falling-out between two people.
이유 없이 ('without reason') is a frequent partner that frames the hatred as unfair.
examples: 저는 아무도 미워하지 않아요
I don't hate anyone
아무도 ('nobody') must pair with the negative 하지 않아요 — Korean double-marks the negative.
한때 동생을 미워했어요
I hated my younger sibling for a while
한때 ('at one time') plus past 미워했어요 softens it into a feeling that has since passed.
우리 이제 그만 서로 미워하지 마세요
Let's stop hating each other now
그만 ('stop / no more') with the polite 하지 마세요 is a gentle plea to end a feud.
nuance: 미워하다 means to actively feel hatred or resentment toward a person, and it is built from the adjective 밉다 ('to be hateful / detestable') by the regular pattern 밉다 → 미워 + 하다 (the ㅂ of 밉다 softens to 워). The key boundary English speakers blur is 미워하다 vs 싫어하다: 싫어하다 is broad 'dislike' and works for things, foods, and situations (비를 싫어해요 = I dislike rain), whereas 미워하다 is a hot, personal emotion aimed almost always at a human being — you can 싫어하다 broccoli but you 미워하다 the person who hurt you. Because it is a 하다 verb, it contracts to 미워해요 / past 미워했어요 (not 미워하요), while keeping 하 in 미워할 거예요. Note that 미워하다 is often less harsh than English 'hate': Korean parents and couples use 미워! playfully to mean 'you meanie / I'm mad at you'. The pitfall is reaching for 미워하다 to translate 'I hate this weather/this job' — that needs 싫다/싫어하다; 미워하다 there sounds as if you bear the weather a grudge.
mistakes: Using 미워하다 for disliking a thing ('I hate kimchi') — things take 싫어하다; 미워하다 is for resenting people.
Writing 미워하요 instead of 미워해요 — as a 하다 verb it must contract 하 + 여 to 해.
Assuming 미워해 always means strong 'hate'; between close people it is often a light, sulky 'you meanie', so don't read it as literal hatred.

usage: A place or absent person takes 을/를 with the verb 그리워하다 (≠ the adjective 그립다, which takes 이/가).
to long for the old days
옛날 ('the old days') is a classic object — 그리워하다 carries a nostalgic, wistful tone.
to miss the one who left
Often used of someone gone or far away, with a deeper ache than everyday 보고 싶다.
몹시 ('terribly') is the natural intensifier; 많이 그리워하다 also works for 'miss a lot'.
examples: 저는 한국 음식을 그리워해요
I miss Korean food
Everyday line when living abroad; the food takes the object marker 을.
그는 옛 친구들을 그리워했어요
He missed his old friends
Third person + past 그리워했어요 — describing someone else's longing, which is exactly when 그리워하다 (not 그립다) is required.
너무 그리워하지 마, 곧 만날 거야
Don't miss them too much, you'll meet soon
반말 comfort: 그리워하지 마 tells a friend not to pine.
nuance: 그리워하다 is the action verb 'to miss / long for / yearn after', formed from the adjective 그립다 ('to be missed') via 그립다 → 그리워 + 하다. The single most important point is the adjective-vs-verb split that trips up English speakers, who have only one word 'miss': use the adjective 그립다 for your own felt state, where the missed thing is the grammatical subject (고향이 그리워요 = lit. 'my hometown is missed-to-me' = I'm homesick), and use the verb 그리워하다 when you describe someone actively missing something, taking an 을/를 object (동생이 고향을 그리워해요). The other near-synonym is 보고 싶다 ('want to see / miss'): 보고 싶다 is light, common, and aimed at people you can still meet (엄마 보고 싶어), while 그리워하다 is more literary and wistful, often for what is gone, distant, or past — you 그리워하다 your childhood, not your friend across town. As a 하다 verb it contracts to 그리워해요 / past 그리워했어요 (never 그리워하요).
mistakes: Saying 내가 고향을 그리워요 — for your own feeling use the adjective with 이/가: 고향이 그리워요; the verb 그리워하다 is for others or takes 을/를.
Treating 보고 싶다 and 그리워하다 as identical — 보고 싶다 is everyday and about people you can meet; 그리워하다 is wistful longing for what's gone or far.
Writing 그리워하요 instead of 그리워해요 — the 하다 stem must contract to 해.

usage: 소원을 빌다 ('wish a wish') is the set phrase for making a wish on a star, candle, or at New Year.
행운을 빌어요 is the everyday Korean equivalent of 'good luck!' / 'fingers crossed'.
Here 빌다 shifts to 'plead / beg' — 용서를 빌다 is to sincerely apologize and ask to be pardoned.
두 손 모아 ('hands brought together') paints the praying gesture; very common in heartfelt wishes.
examples: 새해에 소원을 빌었어요
I made a wish at New Year
Past 빌었어요 — the stem 빌 keeps its ㄹ before the vowel ending 어.
저는 매일 가족의 건강을 빌어요
I pray for my family's health every day
건강을 빌다 ('pray for health') shows the 'pray for' sense aimed at a good outcome.
시험 잘 보라고 행운을 빌어 줄게요
I'll wish you luck on your exam
빌어 주다 ('wish on someone's behalf') + 줄게요 makes it a warm offer to a friend.
nuance: 빌다 spans three related senses — to pray, to make a wish, and to plead/beg — unified by the idea of earnestly asking a higher power or another person for something (소원을 빌다 = make a wish, 행운을 빌다 = wish luck, 용서를 빌다 = beg forgiveness, 잘못을 빌다 = apologize for a wrong). Grammatically it is a ㄹ-irregular verb, and the rule is precise: the stem ㄹ drops only before endings starting with ㄴ, ㅂ, or ㅅ, which is why the formal form is 빕니다 (not 빌습니다) and a noun-modifier is 비는; but before a plain vowel the ㄹ stays, so the polite present is 빌어요 and the past is 빌었어요. A frequent pitfall is overusing the doubled future — it is 빌 거예요, with a single ㄹ, because the ㄹ does not double here. The biggest meaning trap is confusing 빌다 with 빌리다: in modern Korean 빌다 never means 'borrow' — that is exclusively 빌리다 (책을 빌리다 = borrow a book), so 'can I borrow this?' is 빌릴 수 있어요?, not 빌 수 있어요?. For prayer in a strictly religious sense Koreans also say 기도하다, but 빌다 is the warmer, folk word for wishing.
mistakes: Writing the formal form as 빌습니다 — as a ㄹ-irregular the ㄹ drops before ㅂ, giving 빕니다.
Confusing 빌다 (pray / wish / beg) with 빌리다 (borrow) — to borrow a book is 책을 빌리다, never 책을 빌다.
Doubling the ㄹ in the future as 빌 거예요 is correct, but learners often over-drop it to 비 거예요 — keep one ㄹ before 거예요.

usage: 키우다 is the default verb for keeping a pet — Korean 'has' a pet by 'raising' it, not by 가지다.
The core sense: bringing up a child; 잘 키우다 = to raise well.
Figurative — 키우다 also means to grow abilities, confidence, or a business bigger.
A warm collocation: 꿈을 키우다 means to grow and cherish an ambition over time.
examples: 저는 고양이를 키워요
I have (raise) a cat
The everyday way to say you keep a pet — note the object marker 를 on the animal.
부모님이 저를 키워 주셨어요
My parents raised me
키워 주다 (did the raising for me) + honorific 시 → 키워 주셨어요, a respectful way to credit your parents.
회사를 더 크게 키우고 싶어요
I want to grow the company bigger
키우다 + 크게 shows the 'make it grow' sense applied to a business.
nuance: 키우다 is the causative of 크다 ('to be big') — literally 'to make (something) grow / get bigger' — and it stretches across raising children, keeping pets, growing plants, and figuratively building skills, dreams, businesses, even bad habits (병을 키우다 = let an illness worsen). Conjugation is the 우-contraction, not an irregular: the stem 키우 ends in the vowel ㅜ, and ㅜ + 어 fuses into 워, so the casual form is 키워, polite 키워요, and past 키웠어요 (never 키우어요). Compared with its near-twin 기르다, the two overlap heavily for pets, plants, and children, but usage splits by habit: 키우다 is the more colloquial everyday choice for pets and for 'growing bigger' (실력을 키우다), while 기르다 sounds slightly more formal and is preferred for hair, beard, and nails (머리를 기르다, not 머리를 키우다). The classic English-speaker pitfall is using 가지다 ('to have/own') for a pet because English says 'I have a dog' — Korean instead says 강아지를 키워요, since you raise the animal rather than possess it.
mistakes: Writing 키우어요 instead of 키워요 — the stem-final ㅜ contracts with 어 to 워.
Saying 강아지를 가지고 있어요 for 'I have a dog' — Koreans say 강아지를 키워요; 가지다 is for objects, not living pets.
Using 키우다 for growing hair (머리를 키우다) — hair, beard, and nails take 기르다 (머리를 기르다).

usage: 머리를 기르다 is the set phrase for letting hair grow long — 기르다 is preferred over 키우다 here.
Like hair, facial hair 'grows' with 기르다, not 키우다.
Figurative — 좋은 습관을 기르다 / 실력을 기르다 means to cultivate habits or ability over time.
체력/끈기/인내심을 기르다 — 기르다 partners with inner qualities you cultivate.
examples: 저는 수염을 길러요
I'm growing a beard
Note the casual present 길러 — the 르 doubles to ㄹㄹ before the vowel.
할머니께서 채소를 기르세요
My grandmother grows vegetables
Honorific 께서 + 기르세요 raises the subject respectfully.
어릴 때부터 좋은 습관을 길러야 해요
You should build good habits from a young age
기르다 in its 'cultivate' sense, with 야 해요 ('should').
nuance: 기르다 means to grow, raise, rear, or cultivate, and it reaches further into the abstract than its partner 키우다 — beyond plants, animals, and children it readily takes hair, beard, nails (머리/수염/손톱을 기르다) and inner qualities like habits, stamina, patience, and skill (습관을/체력을/실력을 기르다). It is a textbook 르-irregular verb: before an 아/어 ending the 르 splits and an extra ㄹ is inserted into the previous syllable, so 기르 + 어 becomes 길러 (not 기러), giving polite 길러요 and past 길렀어요 with a doubled ㄹ; before consonant endings it stays regular (기르고, 기릅니다, 기를 거예요). Against 키우다 the dividing line is register and collocation: they are interchangeable for pets, plants, and kids, but 키우다 is the more casual, spoken default and owns 'grow bigger' (실력을 키우다 too), whereas 기르다 feels a touch more formal and is the fixed choice for body hair and for written 'cultivate'. The recurring mistake is regularizing the past to 기르었어요 — the 르 irregular forces 길렀어요.
mistakes: Writing the past as 기르었어요 — the 르-irregular gives a doubled ㄹ: 길렀어요.
Dropping the inserted ㄹ in the casual form (기러) — it must be 길러.
Using 키우다 for hair or beard — 머리/수염은 기르다 is the natural collocation, while 키우다 fits pets and 'grow bigger'.

usage: 아기를 낳다 ('give birth to a baby') — the baby takes the object marker 를.
to give birth to a son
Specify the child: 아들/딸을 낳다 for having a son/daughter.
For animals, offspring are 새끼; 고양이가 새끼를 낳다 = the cat has kittens.
자연분만으로 ('by natural delivery') is a common adverbial partner in real talk about childbirth.
examples: 언니가 딸을 낳았어요
My older sister gave birth to a daughter
Past 낳았어요 — the stem ㅎ is kept and ㅏ + 았 attaches normally.
고양이가 새끼를 다섯 마리 낳았어요
The cat had five kittens
낳다 also covers animals; 마리 is the counter for animals.
저는 아이를 둘 낳고 싶어요
I want to have two children
낳고 싶어요 ('want to give birth') — 낳다 keeps its ㅎ before the consonant ending 고.
nuance: 낳다 means to give birth to or bear a child or young, and it is the physical act of delivery — distinct from 키우다/기르다 (raising the child afterward). It is a regular consonant (ㅎ-final) verb, NOT the ㅎ-irregular found in some adjectives, so the ㅎ is always preserved: 낳아요, 낳았어요, 낳습니다 — never 나아요. This is the make-or-break point, because 낳다 looks and sounds almost identical to two other verbs that English speakers constantly mix up: 낫다 ('to recover from illness / be better'), which is ㅅ-irregular and drops to 나아요 (감기가 나았어요 = my cold got better), and 낮다 ('to be low'). So 'I gave birth' is 낳았어요 while 'I got better' is 나았어요 — one keeps ㅎ, the other loses ㅅ. Figuratively 낳다 can also mean 'to produce / give rise to' a result (좋은 결과를 낳다 = bring about a good result). A cultural register note: about a mother one says 낳다, but the polite, formal phrasing for giving birth is often 출산하다, used in hospitals and news; 낳다 is the plain everyday verb.
mistakes: Confusing 낳다 (give birth) with 낫다 (recover) — 'I gave birth' is 낳았어요 (keeps ㅎ), 'I recovered' is 나았어요 (ㅅ drops).
Dropping the ㅎ to write 나아요 for the present — 낳다 is regular, so it is 낳아요.
Using 낳다 for raising a child after birth — that is 키우다/기르다; 낳다 is only the act of giving birth.

A cultural register note: about a mother one says 낳다, but the polite, formal phrasing for giving birth is often 출산하다, used in hospitals and news; 낳다 is the plain everyday verb.
A regular consonant (ㅎ-final) verb, NOT the ㅎ-irregular found in some adjectives, so the ㅎ is always preserved: 낳아요, 낳았어요, 낳습니다 — never 나아요.

낳다 looks and sounds almost identical to two other verbs that English speakers constantly mix up: 낫다 ('to recover from illness / be better'), which is ㅅ-irregular and drops to 나아요 (감기가 나았어요 = my cold got better), and 낮다 ('to be low'). So 'I gave birth' is 낳았어요 (keeps ㅎ) while 'I got better' is 나았어요 (loses ㅅ).

usage: The person you resemble takes 을/를, and Korean states it in the past 닮았어요 for a present fact.
Pair people with 랑/하고/와 to say two people resemble each other: 둘이 닮았어요.
성격이 닮다 — 닮다 covers character, not just looks; the trait takes 이/가.
붕어빵처럼 ('like fish-shaped pastries from the same mold') is the idiom for looking identical.
examples: 아기가 아빠를 많이 닮았어요
The baby looks a lot like the dad
The go-to sentence about family resemblance, with 많이 ('a lot') and past 닮았어요.
저는 할머니를 닮았어요
I take after my grandmother
닮다 covers both appearance and personality — context decides which.
성격이 형하고 정말 닮았어요
My personality really resembles my older brother's
형하고 닮다 ('resemble + with brother') — the partner of resemblance takes 하고.
nuance: 닮다 means to resemble or take after someone in looks or character, and its single most counter-intuitive feature for English speakers is tense: Korean overwhelmingly states a present resemblance in the PAST form 닮았어요, because the resembling is treated as a completed, settled state that holds now — so 엄마를 닮았어요 means 'I look like my mom (right now)', and saying present 닮아요 sounds oddly like an ongoing action and is rare. The grammar of the partners matters too: the person you take after takes the object marker 을/를 (아빠를 닮다), while two people who look alike are linked with 하고/와/과/랑 (형하고 닮다, 둘이 닮다). Distinguish it sharply from 같다 ('to be the same/identical'): 닮다 is partial likeness — a family resemblance — whereas 같다 claims sameness, so 'they look similar' is 닮았어요 but 'they're the same' is 같아요. It is a regular ㄻ-cluster verb (닮아요, 닮았어요, 닮습니다). A vivid native idiom for strong resemblance is 붕어빵처럼 닮았다, like two pastries from one mold.
mistakes: Using the present 닮아요 for 'looks like' — Korean states a current resemblance in the past: 닮았어요.
Choosing 같다 ('be identical') when you mean only a resemblance — that is 닮다; 같다 claims they are the same.
Marking the person with 이/가 (엄마가 닮았어요 to mean 'I look like mom') — the one you resemble takes 을/를: 엄마를 닮았어요.

usage: What looks good on you takes 이/가, not 을/를 — 옷이 어울려요, paired with 잘 ('well').
I get along well with friends
Second sense: 사람들하고 어울리다 = to mingle / socialize with people.
어울리다 also means 'be in keeping with' — 분위기/상황에 어울리다, with 에 on the setting.
잘 어울리는 ('well-matched') modifies a couple or a combination that goes together nicely.
examples: 그 색이 정말 잘 어울려요
That color really suits you
A natural compliment; note 색이 (이/가), since the color is what suits.
이 신발이 치마하고 잘 어울려요
These shoes go well with the skirt
Item + 하고 어울리다 = two things match each other.
저는 새 동료들하고 금방 어울렸어요
I quickly mixed in with the new coworkers
Past 어울렸어요 in the 'get along / fit in' sense, with 금방 ('quickly').
nuance: 어울리다 carries two everyday meanings bound by one idea — 'to harmonize / fit together well': (1) to suit or look good on someone (이 옷이 잘 어울려요 = this suits you), and (2) to mingle, blend in, or get along with people (친구들하고 잘 어울려요). The particle pattern is the crux for English speakers, because English 'suits you' makes 'you' the object: in Korean the thing that suits is the SUBJECT and takes 이/가 (옷이 어울려요, never 옷을 어울려요), the person it suits is unmarked or takes 한테/에게, and a matching partner or group takes 하고/와/과 (치마하고 어울리다, 사람들하고 어울리다); a setting it fits takes 에 (분위기에 어울리다). Conjugation is the regular ㅣ-vowel contraction, not an irregular: 어울리 + 어 fuses to 어울려, giving polite 어울려요 and past 어울렸어요 (not 어울리어요). A useful contrast: 어울리다 ('look good / harmonize') vs 맞다 ('fit in size / be correct') — clothes that 어울리다 flatter you, clothes that 맞다 are the right size, and the two are not the same compliment.
mistakes: Using 을/를 for what suits you — say 옷이 어울려요 (이/가), never 옷을 어울려요; the flattering thing is the subject.
Writing 어울리어요 instead of the contracted 어울려요 — the stem-final ㅣ fuses with 어 to 려.
Confusing 어울리다 (look good / harmonize) with 맞다 (fit in size / be correct) — 'this suits you' is 어울려요, 'this fits (size)' is 맞아요.
